improvement_notes: Clarify the distinction between a grid cell's physical width and the distance between neighboring cell centers. The current wording is correct under the stated model, but a brief diagram label would prevent students from generalizing the formula incorrectly.

In the optional route-comparison example, explicitly state that four right moves followed by two up moves has two direction runs but only one turn. This will prevent confusion between runs, direction changes, and turns.

Add a brief note that the plotted polyline connects cell centers and is not necessarily a collision-free continuous trajectory for a finite-sized robot. The later caveats imply this, but stating it near the first plot would improve technical precision.

The visual instructions in 'See It in Your Head' use generic left-to-right signal language that does not clearly match the path-planning schematic. Replace it with path-specific prompts such as identifying the start, goal, obstacle boundary, route, and safety margin.

The Python lab relies on matplotlib without stating the installation requirement or offering a no-install fallback. Add a short setup note and, if appropriate, a text-only validation alternative for accessibility and classroom portability.

Consider adding one explicit student prediction before the worked route: ask whether the direct Manhattan route intersects the obstacle and which side route might be shortest. This would strengthen the transition from intuition to formal validation.

The lesson mentions unknown occupancy and map uncertainty in the real-robot section but does not connect them to a concrete planning policy. A one-sentence example such as 'treat unknown cells as blocked' would make the engineering implication more actionable.

The lesson is exceptionally complete for an introductory class, but the vocabulary, further-learning, and repeated validation explanations could be trimmed slightly if the course prioritizes shorter class sessions.

linkedin.title: Class 37: Path Planning from Grid Models to Real Robot Safety
linkedin.description: Learn how RoboRover represents routes, validates grid movements, calculates distance, and connects idealized paths to real-world clearance and uncertainty.
linkedin.commentary:
A path on a map is not yet a safe route for a robot.

In Professor OS Class 37, students move from SLAM’s map to the next robotics question: where should the robot drive? They build and validate a grid-based path from a start to a goal while avoiding obstacles.

Students learn to:
• Represent a route as an ordered sequence of positions.
• Verify obstacle avoidance and one-cell movement constraints.
• Calculate planned center-to-center distance.
• Use Python assertions to catch collisions and invalid jumps.
• Recognize why robot width, uncertainty, wheel slip, and changing obstacles matter.

The lesson deliberately separates planning from control: a planner proposes a route, while a controller later turns that route into motor commands. The hands-on lab also shows why checking only listed obstacle cells is insufficient.

Try the lab by designing a second safe route and comparing its length and number of turns with the example. Which route would your robot prefer, and why?
